The city opened its Department of Lost Things on a Tuesday, because Mondays were already responsible for enough.

At first, the department occupied a narrow room behind the tax office. There were shelves for umbrellas, drawers for keys, and a refrigerator for lunches abandoned on buses. A clerk named Mara sat beneath a sign that read:

**IF YOU HAVE LOST SOMETHING, PLEASE DESCRIBE IT WITHOUT EXAGGERATION.**

This proved difficult.

“My wallet,” people said, “with my whole life in it.”

“My wedding ring. It means everything.”

“My phone. I’m literally dead without it.”

Mara would hand them a form.

“Just the object, please.”

For seven years, the work was ordinary. Gloves arrived singly. Earrings glittered in little envelopes. Someone misplaced a trombone, which remained unclaimed despite being difficult to forget.

Then, one rainy afternoon, an elderly man entered carrying nothing.

“I’ve lost the smell of my mother’s kitchen,” he said.

Mara looked up.

“Was it attached to anything?”

“No.”

“Did you lose it on public transport?”

“I don’t think so.”

He stood quietly while rain ticked against the window.

“She used to burn the butter a little,” he added. “Not badly. Just enough.”

Mara should have sent him away. Instead, she gave him a form.

Under *Description of Item*, he wrote: *Warm. Slightly bitter. Before anything bad happened.*

That evening, while locking the cabinet of watches, Mara smelled butter browning in a pan.

Behind the cabinet stood a small blue door.

It had not been there that morning.

Mara opened it.

Inside was a kitchen, though not exactly a kitchen. There were no walls, only the suggestion of wallpaper. A woman’s voice hummed beyond sight. On the stove, butter foamed in a blackened skillet.

Mara closed the door carefully.

The next day, she called the elderly man.

He stayed inside for eleven minutes.

When he came out, he was crying, but he looked less tired.

“Can I take it home?”

“I don’t know how you would.”

He nodded. Before leaving, he asked whether he might return sometime.

Word spread.

Soon people came looking for things no shelf could hold: the courage they had possessed at nineteen, a language they had stopped speaking, the feeling of being expected somewhere.

The department moved into an abandoned railway station.

New doors appeared nightly.

Behind one lay the summer before a brother died. Behind another, the precise silence following a snowfall in a village that no longer existed. One room contained nothing but the conviction that tomorrow would be better.

That room was always booked.

Mara hired assistants. They developed procedures.

No flame was allowed near recovered anger. Lost afternoons had to be stored flat. Childhood friendships were fragile and could not be exposed to fluorescent light.

Some items remained stubbornly missing.

Nobody found the right words for the last conversation.

Nobody recovered time in usable quantities.

People complained about this.

“I pay taxes,” one man said.

Mara agreed that he probably did.

There were dangers, too.

A woman found her first love and refused to leave the room. A violinist recovered his ambition, only to discover it no longer fit inside his life. A father asked for his daughter’s trust, but the department could locate only the moment he had broken it.

“We don’t manufacture things,” Mara told him.

He stayed sitting across from her long after she finished speaking.

Years passed. Mara’s hair silvered. The station filled with doors.

Every morning she checked the arrivals ledger. Every evening she walked the corridors, listening for leaks. Once, an unattended room spilled three hours of Sunday happiness into the main hall, and everyone missed their train without minding.

Mara herself filed no requests.

She considered this professionalism.

Her assistants considered it suspicious.

“You must have lost something,” said Ivo, the youngest.

“Of course.”

“Then why not look?”

She capped her pen.

“Someone has to keep the office open.”

One winter, a package appeared on her desk.

It was wrapped in brown paper and addressed in her own handwriting, though she did not remember writing it.

Inside lay a small brass key.

Attached was a note:

*You are allowed to miss what you chose to leave.*

Mara sat down.

Before the department, before the tax office, there had been a house near the sea. There had been a man who laughed with his whole face. There had been plans involving a garden, a dog, a table large enough for friends.

She had left.

The leaving had been necessary.

This had not made it painless.

For thirty years, she had confused regretting the loss with regretting the decision. Whenever a good memory surfaced, she rehearsed the reasons she had gone until it sank again.

At the end of the western corridor, a door waited.

The key turned easily.

Inside, the sea breathed against a shore of pale stones.

There was the house, its windows lit. There was the garden they had never planted. She could hear him laughing somewhere indoors.

Mara stood on the path.

She did not enter.

Instead, she sat on the low wall and watched the water darken.

For the first time in years, she remembered an ordinary happy evening without making herself account for it. They had eaten outside. He had dropped a fork between the boards of the deck. Neither of them had wanted to get up and fetch another.

She stayed until she was cold.

In the morning, Mara changed the sign above the front desk.

It now read:

**IF YOU HAVE LOST SOMETHING, YOU MAY DESCRIBE IT AS BEST YOU CAN.**

Below that, in smaller letters, she added:

**FINDING IT DOES NOT OBLIGE YOU TO TAKE IT BACK.**

Then she unlocked the station doors.

Outside, people waited in the cold, holding photographs, empty boxes, and one unremarkable umbrella.

Mara welcomed them in.
